blocks.text: Acts 19 narrates Paul's extended mission in Ephesus through three distinct phases. First, he encounters disciples who knew only John's baptism and reorients them through baptism into Jesus's name, with the Holy Spirit's gift followed by tongues and prophecy. Second, he teaches in the synagogue for three months, then withdraws to the school of Tyrannus for two years of daily dialogue, resulting in broad regional hearing. Third, the narrative distinguishes Paul's healings through objects from failed attempts by Jewish exorcists to invoke Jesus's name. Throughout, Acts preserves different settings, practitioners, and ritual outcomes without imposing a single normative pattern of spiritual reception or constructing universal institutions.

sections.title: Reception and Baptism of John's Disciples (19:1-7)

blocks.text: Paul finds approximately twelve believers in Ephesus who had received only John's baptism. When asked whether they received the Holy Spirit, they report never having heard of the Spirit's giving. John's baptism, according to Acts, emphasized repentance and belief in the coming figure—Jesus—but these disciples had not received instruction about or experienced the Spirit's arrival. After Paul's explanation, they are baptized into Jesus's name. Paul then lays hands on them; the Holy Spirit comes upon them, and they speak in tongues and prophesy. Acts reports this sequence without prescribing it as the sole or necessary pattern. Elsewhere in Acts, the Spirit arrives at varied points in the conversion process—sometimes before water baptism, sometimes after, sometimes accompanied by visible signs, sometimes not. This passage exemplifies one sequence among several, indicating transition from John's preparatory movement to full Christ-community formation.

Paul's Ephesian teaching unfolds in two distinct settings. For three months he enters the synagogue, speaks boldly, and reasons and persuades concerning the kingdom of God. This setting places him within a diaspora Jewish venue for scriptural debate and instruction. When opposition emerges—some becoming hardened and speaking evil of the Way before crowds—Paul withdraws the disciples and relocates to the school of Tyrannus. Acts names this venue without describing its organization or Tyrannus's role. Paul continues daily reasoning there for two years. The summary states that all dwelt in Asia heard the Lord's word, both Jews and Greeks. This claim indicates regional scope and impact without providing a census or mechanism of spread. The shift from synagogue to the named urban venue reflects real distinctions in early Christian teaching arrangements without establishing Tyrannus as a formal school proprietor or proving conversion of all who heard.

Acts attributes special miracles to Paul as God's work. The sick are healed and evil spirits depart when handkerchiefs or aprons touched to Paul's body are brought to afflicted persons. This portrayal associates Pauline healing with physical objects and divine agency. The narrative then shifts to itinerant Jewish exorcists—a distinct group. Seven men, sons of a Jew named Sceva and described as a chief priest, attempt to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over possessed persons. They say, 'I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.' Their invocation differs from Pauline healing: they use Jesus's name as a formula or power without apparent relationship or authority. The evil spirit responds by acknowledging Jesus and Paul but questioning the exorcists' identity. The possessed man overpowers all seven, defeats them, and they flee naked. Acts differentiates the outcomes: Pauline healing succeeds; attempted name-invocation by unrelated practitioners fails, lacking spiritual authority or relationship. The narrative does not claim magic was inherent to exorcism practice or to any ethnic group, nor does it identify the source of materials destroyed in subsequent verses.

Acts frames the Ephesian mission within first-century diaspora Judaism, synagogue debate, scriptural instruction, and the presence of Jewish ritual specialists. The synagogue setting and the mention of Jewish exorcists situate the narrative in a world where Jewish religious practice, scriptural tradition, and competing claims to spiritual authority were part of urban life. Jewish and non-Jewish participants appear as distinct groups with differing responses to Paul's message. These details contextualize Acts' account without establishing uniform backgrounds among all Ephesian believers or fixing religious categories rigidly.
